URL: https://www.theguardian.com/money/2026/nov/22/black-friday-scam-deals--ai-fake-storefront
The Guardian, 22 Nov 2026 07:00 GMT

AI is being used to clone retailers’ sites and ‘poison’ chatbots into recommending them,  experts say

Prefer the Guardian on GoogleBlack Friday is coming so you search online for the coat you have been after in the hope you can get it at a good price. Within a few minutes, you find just the right one, in the colour you want and at a huge discount.

You decide to take advantage of the bargain quickly and transfer the money then wait for it to be delivered.

But the coat will never arrive as you have fallen victim to a sophisticated “fake storefront” that has the appearance of a legitimate brand site – including having the name in the url – but is in fact an AI-created clone of the real thing.

As shoppers start searching for bargains before Black Friday on 27 November, cybersecurity professionals are warning of an increase in clone websites, designed to steal your money or card details.

The antivirus company Norton says it expects the number of suspect sites to rise significantly as the gift-buying season gets into full swing.

“The increase is clear every year at this time between Black Friday and Christmas,” says Luis Corrons, a security researcher from Norton.

These fake sites can emerge in regular search results and also in the results from AI chatbots. National Trading Standards has said that criminals are “poisoning” AI models, such as ChatGPT, so they produce scam websites in their results and recommend them to users.

Michael Vainshtein, a co-founder of the security company Guardio, says this is achieved through fake shopfronts and phishing pages. “They reach [AI] agents the same way they reach people: through populating search results, Google ads and other paid ads, compromised sites and social posts pushing a hot sale,” he says.

Leyla Bilge, the global head of scam research at Norton, says young people should pay particular attention to the potential for fraud as they are more likely to come across scams on social media or to act on impulse.

“If a hard-to-find item suddenly turns up cheap from a seller you’ve never heard of, treat that as a warning sign rather than a stroke of luck,” she says.

Cloned websites are frequently created using AI and can look identical to the real thing. The goods listed will often have huge discounts attached – for example, 80% in some cases – in a bid to lure people in.

They often have a convincingly similar web address. In June, the Guardian showed how websites designed to look like the shoe seller Russell & Bromley had URLs including therussellbromleyofficial and russellbromleyonlineuk.

When you get to the payment page you may be asked for your card details, but you will usually be asked to pay by a bank transfer or maybe cryptocurrency. Sometimes you will be offered the option to use PayPal, but be steered towards the “send to a friend” option and told this is to avoid fees.

Look at the web address of the page you land on – legitimate UK sites will often use .co.uk or .com. And beware of extras words in the title such as “official” or “deals”.

An immediate red flag is if they only take payment by bank transfer or with cryptocurrency.

The Co-operative Bank has just launched a new tool whereby you can upload any suspicious text, email or website and it will tell you whether it is safe or not.

If you realise that you have handed over your financial details, report it to your bank and Report Fraud.

You can report sites that violate ChatGPT policies through this form.
